newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade to seek new delay on IMF re-entry.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade to seek new delay on IMF re-entry.

text.p: Yugoslavia, citing outstanding liabilities and problems, said on Saturday it would seek a further six-month delay in any decision on readmission to the International Monetary Fund, from which it was expelled five years ago.

"We shall ask the IMF to postpone any decision on our membership for another six months and expect that our request will be granted," Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic told Reuters on return from a trip to the United States.

Last December, the IMF board of directors postponed discussion on Yugoslavia's membership until June 14, as a routine measure taken twice a year since 1992. Belgrade is widely held responsible for precipitating the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and its expulsion from the IMF took place amid a series of other international sanctions against it.

Yugoslavia's return to the IMF and the World Bank remains conditional on its cooperation with the Hague international war crimes tribunal, respect for human rights in its mostly ethnic Albanian province of Kosovo and progress in talks on dividing former Yugoslavia's assets.
Rejoining the IMF, World Bank and other institutions is seen as crucial for the country to get renewed access to foreign funds urgently needed to repair its moribund economy.

Djunic, in charge of economic reforms and relations with world financial bodies, and Yugoslav IMF Minister Nebojsa Maljkovic, spent a week in New York and Washington unofficially meeting representatives of the IMF and the World Bank.
On their return on Saturday, the two ministers cautioned against any premature optimism.

"We have not yet finished the entire work on an expert level. There are many details, we have our liabilities towards the IMF, World Bank, London Club, and they are linked with all other liabilities and problems that we have," Djunic said.
"It is a delicate job to find a mutually acceptable starting point for regulating the entire problem," he added.
Yugoslav officials also met the president of the London club of commercial creditors and agreed to hold a new round of talks with an expert group representing it in London on June 23.
Yugoslavia, among the last East European country with commercial debt restructuring still to be rescheduled, last held technical talks with commercial creditors late last year.

Sources close to the negotiating team said the talks stumbled over Belgrade presenting an overly optimistic report on the country's economic situation. Some of the major issues hanging over the talks are how Belgrade plans to share former Yugoslavia's assets with the other successor republics and the issue of its IMF membership.
